title: Module 3: Sound Waves and Acoustic Parameters

questions.stem: A wave is best defined as:
options: A movement of matter from one place to another
A vibration that stays in one place
A mechanism that transfers energy without permanently displacing matter
A flow of particles through a medium
questions.explanation: A wave transfers energy from one location to another without permanently displacing matter.

questions.stem: Ultrasound waves are cyclical because they are produced by:
options: A repetitive electrical signal in the transducer
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is produced by a repetitive electrical signal applied to the transducer, creating repeated cycles.

questions.stem: In wave terminology, a "cycle" is:
questions.explanation: A cycle is one complete oscillation; "cyclical" means repeated cycles.

questions.stem: As a wave passes through a medium, the particles:
options: Oscillate around their resting positions without travelling with the wave
questions.explanation: Energy moves through the medium while particles only oscillate around their resting positions.

questions.stem: Greater wave amplitude is associated with:
questions.explanation: Greater amplitude is associated with greater wave energy.

questions.stem: Mechanical waves:
options: Consist of electric and magnetic fields
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves need a material medium and transfer energy through particle interaction.

questions.stem: Which wave cannot travel through a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Sound is mechanical and cannot travel through a vacuum. Light, X-rays and radio waves can.

questions.stem: Which is an electromagnetic wave?
questions.explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic waves (changing electric and magnetic fields).

questions.stem: Ultrasound is a:
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is a mechanical wave and needs tissue or another medium.

questions.stem: Sound is best described as:
options: A pressure wave created by a mechanical action
questions.explanation: Sound is a pressure wave created by a mechanical action (a vibrating source).

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the five important characteristics of sound?
options: Sound is a wave that transfers energy
Sound requires a medium to propagate
Sound travels in straight paths through a uniform medium
questions.explanation: Sound is mechanical, not electromagnetic.

questions.stem: In soft tissue, ultrasound is a:
questions.explanation: Sound is longitudinal in soft tissue.

questions.stem: Sound travels in straight paths through:
questions.explanation: Sound travels in straight paths through a uniform medium.

questions.stem: A vibrating source causes a wave to propagate because:
options: The source moves through the tissue
Intermolecular forces transfer the disturbance to neighbouring particles
Particles travel from the source to the receiver
questions.explanation: Intermolecular forces pass the disturbance to neighbouring particles, so the wave propagates.

questions.stem: Which list contains the four acoustic variables?
questions.explanation: The four acoustic variables are pressure, density, particle motion and temperature.

questions.stem: Which is NOT an acoustic variable?
questions.explanation: Wavelength is an acoustic parameter, not an acoustic variable.

questions.stem: The unit of pressure is:
questions.explanation: Pressure is force per unit area, measured in pascals (Pa).

questions.stem: The unit of density is:
questions.explanation: Density is mass per unit volume, measured in kg/m³.

questions.stem: Particle motion (displacement) is measured in:
questions.explanation: Particle motion is displacement from the resting position, in metres.

questions.stem: If the resting value of a wave is 20 pascals, the acoustic variable is:
questions.explanation: Pascals are the unit of pressure.

questions.stem: If the resting value of a wave is 19 kg/m³, the acoustic variable is:
questions.explanation: kg/m³ is the unit of density.

questions.stem: In a transverse wave, the particles move:
questions.explanation: Transverse waves have particle motion perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

questions.stem: Transverse waves are often called:
questions.explanation: Transverse waves are often called shear waves.

questions.stem: A wave along a stretched rope is an example of a:
options: Standing sound wave in soft tissue
questions.explanation: A rope wave is the classic transverse wave example.

questions.stem: In a longitudinal wave, the particles move:
questions.explanation: In longitudinal waves, particles move parallel to wave propagation.

questions.stem: Longitudinal waves produce alternating:
options: Crests and troughs of particle travel
questions.explanation: Longitudinal waves create alternating compressions and rarefactions.

questions.stem: A compression is a region of:
questions.explanation: Compressions have particles closer together: higher density and higher pressure.

questions.stem: A rarefaction is a region of:
questions.explanation: Rarefactions have particles farther apart: lower density and lower pressure.

questions.stem: The sine wave used to display sound is:
options: The actual path of the particles
A graph of an acoustic variable over time or distance
questions.explanation: The sine wave is a graph of an acoustic variable, not the path of the particles.

questions.stem: On a pressure sine wave, crests represent:
questions.explanation: Crests represent maximum compression pressure.

questions.stem: On a pressure sine wave, troughs represent:
questions.explanation: Troughs represent maximum rarefaction pressure.

questions.stem: How many acoustic parameters of sound are listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The seven parameters are frequency, period, wavelength, propagation speed, amplitude, power and intensity.

questions.stem: Frequency is defined as:
options: The number of cycles per second
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of cycles per second.

questions.stem: The unit of frequency is:
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz (1/second).

questions.stem: Diagnostic ultrasound frequencies are expressed in:
questions.explanation: Diagnostic ultrasound uses megahertz (MHz).

questions.stem: Frequency is determined by the:
questions.explanation: Frequency is determined by the sound source (the transducer crystal).

questions.stem: According to the lecture, is frequency changed by the sonographer?
options: No – it is determined by the sound source
questions.explanation: The lecture lists frequency as determined by the source and not changed by the sonographer.

questions.stem: Infrasound has a frequency:
questions.explanation: Infrasound is below 20 Hz.

questions.stem: Audible sound ranges from:
questions.explanation: Audible sound is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

questions.stem: Ultrasound is defined as sound with a frequency:
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is above 20,000 Hz.

questions.stem: Conventional diagnostic ultrasound uses frequencies of about:
questions.explanation: Conventional diagnostic ultrasound is about 2–20 MHz.

questions.stem: Higher-frequency sound provides:
questions.explanation: Higher frequency gives better resolution but more attenuation and less penetration.

questions.stem: Lower-frequency sound provides:
questions.explanation: Lower frequency penetrates deeper but gives lower resolution.

questions.stem: Higher-frequency sound has:
questions.explanation: Wavelength = c/f, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

questions.stem: Period is:
options: The number of cycles per second
The time required for one cycle
questions.explanation: Period is the time required for one cycle.

questions.stem: A common unit for the period of ultrasound is the:
questions.explanation: Periods of diagnostic ultrasound are in microseconds.

questions.stem: Frequency and period are:
questions.explanation: f = 1/T and T = 1/f.

questions.stem: A 2 MHz wave has a period of:
questions.explanation: T = 1/2 MHz = 0.5 µs.

questions.stem: Propagation speed is determined by:
questions.explanation: Propagation speed is set by the medium, not the transducer.

questions.stem: The symbol and common unit of propagation speed are:
questions.explanation: Propagation speed uses symbol c, in m/s or mm/µs.

questions.stem: The average speed of sound in soft tissue is about:
questions.explanation: The soft tissue average is about 1540 m/s.

questions.stem: Which medium has the slowest propagation speed?
questions.explanation: Of the listed media, lung (air-containing) is the slowest.

questions.stem: In which state of matter is sound fastest?
questions.explanation: Sound is fastest in solids, intermediate in liquids and slowest in gases.

questions.stem: Does propagation speed depend on frequency?
options: No, it is independent of frequency
questions.explanation: Propagation speed is independent of frequency.

questions.stem: Wavelength is:
options: The number of cycles per second
The distance occupied by one cycle
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance occupied by one cycle.

questions.stem: Which equation gives wavelength?
questions.explanation: λ = c / f.

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of a 3 MHz pulse in soft tissue (c = 1540 m/s)?
What is the wavelength of a 1 MHz wave in bone (c = 4080 m/s)?
What is the wavelength of a 5 MHz wave in soft tissue?
What is the wavelength of a 2 MHz wave in soft tissue?
What is the wavelength of a 10 MHz wave in soft tissue?
For the same frequency, which wave has the longer wavelength?
questions.explanation: Sound travels faster in soft tissue than in fat, so at the same frequency its wavelength is longer.

questions.stem: If frequency doubles in the same medium, wavelength:
questions.explanation: λ = c/f, so doubling f halves λ.

questions.stem: At the same frequency, a higher propagation speed gives a:
questions.explanation: At constant frequency, λ = c/f increases when c increases.

questions.stem: Which properties of a medium determine propagation speed?
options: Elasticity, compressibility, stiffness and bulk modulus
questions.explanation: Speed depends on the medium's elasticity, compressibility, stiffness and bulk modulus.

questions.stem: Bulk modulus is a measure of:
questions.explanation: Bulk modulus measures stiffness: how much pressure is needed to compress the material.

questions.stem: A material with a high bulk modulus is:
questions.explanation: High bulk modulus means stiff, incompressible and inelastic.

questions.stem: Bulk modulus is ______ to compressibility.
questions.explanation: Low compressibility means high bulk modulus, so they are inversely proportional.

questions.stem: A high bulk modulus results in:
questions.explanation: High bulk modulus means high propagation speed.

questions.stem: Bone has a very fast sound speed mainly because it is:
questions.explanation: Bone is very stiff (and dense), giving a very fast sound speed.

questions.stem: Two media have the same density but different compressibility. The more compressible medium has:
questions.explanation: Higher compressibility means lower bulk modulus and lower speed. The statement that the more compressible medium is faster is false.

questions.stem: Soft tissue propagates sound faster than air mainly because soft tissue is:
questions.explanation: Soft tissue is much stiffer than air. The speed difference is not explained by density alone.

questions.stem: In the train analogy, the slack between cars represents:
questions.explanation: Slack between cars represents compressibility.

questions.stem: In the train analogy, more slack causes:
questions.explanation: More slack (more compressible) means slower propagation.

questions.stem: In the train analogy, tight coupling between cars causes:
questions.explanation: Tight coupling (stiff) means faster propagation.

questions.stem: In the train analogy, a heavier (greater mass) train gives:
questions.explanation: A heavier train accelerates more slowly, so the wave propagates more slowly.

questions.stem: Can the sonographer directly adjust propagation speed?
questions.explanation: Propagation speed depends on the medium, so the sonographer cannot directly adjust it.

questions.stem: Compared with soft tissue, sound in gases is:
questions.explanation: Gases are slower than soft tissue.

questions.stem: If frequency increases in the same medium, propagation speed:
questions.explanation: Speed is independent of frequency within the same medium.

questions.stem: If frequency increases, the period:
questions.explanation: T = 1/f, so higher frequency means a shorter period.

questions.stem: The relationship between speed, frequency and wavelength is:
questions.explanation: c = f × λ.

questions.stem: Amplitude is formally defined as the:
options: Maximum variation of an acoustic variable from its mean
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum variation of a variable from its mean.

questions.stem: In ultrasound, amplitude often refers to the:
options: Transmit voltage exciting the crystal (unit: volts)
questions.explanation: In ultrasound, amplitude often refers to the transmit voltage that excites the crystal, in volts.

questions.stem: Which expression gives amplitude?
questions.explanation: Amplitude = (max − min)/2 (also max − mean, or mean − min).

questions.stem: A wave has a maximum of 12 and a minimum of 4. Its amplitude is:
Overall (receiver) gain:
questions.explanation: Overall (receiver) gain amplifies all returning echoes equally and affects image brightness.

questions.stem: Time gain compensation (TGC):
options: Adjusts gain at different depths to compensate for attenuation
questions.explanation: TGC adjusts gain at different depths to compensate for attenuation.

questions.stem: Increasing transmit power changes the:
options: Amplitude of the sound leaving the probe
questions.explanation: Transmit gain (power) changes the amplitude of the sound leaving the probe.

questions.stem: Power is:
options: The rate of acoustic energy transfer
The number of cycles per second
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of acoustic energy transfer (watts).

questions.stem: Power is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Power is proportional to amplitude squared.

questions.stem: If the transmit voltage (amplitude) is doubled, power:
questions.explanation: 2² = 4, so doubling amplitude quadruples power.

questions.stem: Intensity is:
questions.explanation: I = P / A.

questions.stem: A beam has a power of 2 W over an area of 4 cm². Its intensity is:
questions.explanation: 2 W ÷ 4 cm² = 0.5 W/cm².

questions.stem: If the beam area gets smaller while power stays constant, intensity:
questions.explanation: Smaller area means higher intensity.

questions.stem: In a sound beam, intensity is greatest where the beam is:
questions.explanation: Intensity is greatest where the beam is narrow.

questions.stem: As sound propagates through tissue, amplitude, power and intensity:
questions.explanation: All three strength parameters weaken as sound propagates through tissue.

questions.stem: Interference occurs when:
options: Two waves meet and their pressure changes combine
questions.explanation: Interference occurs when two waves meet and their pressure changes combine.

questions.stem: Constructive interference occurs when waves are:
options: In phase, so peaks align with peaks and amplitudes add
questions.explanation: In-phase waves (peaks with peaks) add, giving a larger amplitude.

questions.stem: Destructive interference occurs when waves are:
options: Out of phase, so amplitudes subtract
questions.explanation: Out-of-phase waves overlap positive with negative pressure, so amplitudes subtract.

questions.stem: Complete destructive interference requires waves that have:
options: Equal amplitudes and are in phase
Equal amplitudes and are 180° out of phase
questions.explanation: Complete cancellation needs equal amplitudes that are exactly out of phase (180°).
